question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Geeta was working now but she can be seen swimming in the river every evening.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Geeta was working now.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence mixes two different tenses inappropriately: "was working now" (Past Continuous) is used together with "can be seen swimming...every evening" (Simple Present, describing a habitual action).

• Rule — Time expressions and tense agreement: The adverb "now" refers to the present moment and must be used with the Present Continuous Tense (is/am/are + V-ing), never with the Past Continuous Tense (was/were + V-ing).

• The segment should correctly read "Geeta is working now" to agree with the time marker "now" and to make logical sense with the rest of the sentence, which describes her current situation and habitual evening activity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "swimming in the" is correct as it is; it is part of the correctly formed Present Tense verb phrase "can be seen swimming".

• Option 2: "river every evening." is correct as it is; "every evening" correctly signals a habitual action taking the Simple Present Tense.

• Option 3: "but she can be seen" is correct as it is; "can be seen" is a grammatically valid Simple Present passive modal construction.

NOTE

• Time expressions like "now", "at present", "at this moment" always take the Continuous form of the tense that matches the time frame (Present Continuous for present time).

• Time expressions like "every day/evening", "usually", "always", "often" signal habitual actions and require the Simple Present Tense.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The manager asked / the cooking team, “Who / among you is to baked the / Christmas cake this year?”
option_3: among you is to baked the
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. among you is to baked the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment contains the error "is to baked"; after the structure "to be + to" (expressing a plan, arrangement, or duty), the verb that follows "to" must be in its base form (V1), not the past tense/past participle form.

• Rule — Infinitive form after "to": Whenever "to" is used as part of an infinitive (to + verb), the verb must remain in its base form, e.g. "to bake", "to go", "to eat" — never "to baked", "to went", "to ate".

• The segment should correctly read "among you is to bake the".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Christmas cake this year?”" is correct as it is; it is simply the object phrase completing the question with correct punctuation.

• Option 2: "The manager asked" is correct as it is; it is a grammatically correct reporting clause in the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 4: "the cooking team, “Who" is correct as it is; it correctly introduces the quoted question with proper punctuation.

NOTE

• Common infinitive errors tested by SSC include using a past form or a gerund after "to" where a base verb is required, e.g. "wants to going" (incorrect) vs "wants to go" (correct).

• Modal-like structures such as "is/am/are + to + V1" are used to express a formal arrangement, plan, or instruction (e.g. "You are to submit the report by Friday").

question:
Select the grammatically INCORRECT sentence.
They often meet each other.
They always meet each other.
They quite meet each other.
They hardly meet each other.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. They quite meet each other.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "quite" is an adverb of degree that is normally used to modify adjectives, adverbs, or nouns (e.g. "quite good", "quite well", "quite a surprise") — it is not used directly before an ordinary action verb like "meet" to indicate frequency.

• Rule — Adverbs of frequency vs adverbs of degree: Words like "often", "always", "hardly", "rarely", "usually" are adverbs of frequency and can be placed before a main verb to show how often an action happens. "Quite", being a degree adverb, cannot grammatically perform this role.

• Because "quite" cannot logically or grammatically modify the verb "meet" in this way, the sentence "They quite meet each other" is grammatically incorrect and does not convey a sensible meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "They often meet each other." is correct; "often" is a valid adverb of frequency correctly placed before the main verb.

• Option 2: "They always meet each other." is correct; "always" is a valid adverb of frequency correctly placed before the main verb.

• Option 4: "They hardly meet each other." is correct; "hardly" is a valid adverb of frequency (meaning "rarely") correctly placed before the main verb.

NOTE

• Common adverbs of frequency placed before the main verb (but after "to be"): always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, seldom, hardly, never.

• "Quite" is correctly used as in: "She is quite intelligent", "He quite enjoyed the movie" (modifying an adjective/verb-phrase of degree, not indicating frequency).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The new / secretary / does not likes / me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. does not likes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment contains the error "does not likes"; when the auxiliary verb "does" (used for third-person singular subjects in the Simple Present Tense, negative form) is present, the main verb that follows must be in its base form (V1), without the "-s/-es" ending.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense (negative, third-person singular): Subject + does not + V1 (e.g. "He does not like", "She does not go") — the "-s" is carried only by "does", not repeated on the main verb.

• The segment should correctly read "does not like".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "me." is correct as it is; it is simply the object of the verb "like".

• Option 2: "secretary" is correct as it is; it is part of the correctly formed subject "The new secretary".

• Option 3: "The new" is correct as it is; it is a correctly formed adjective phrase modifying "secretary".

NOTE

• This is one of the most frequently tested SSC error-spotting patterns: double marking of the third-person "-s" on both the auxiliary ("does/is/has") and the main verb, e.g. "He does not knows" (incorrect) vs "He does not know" (correct).

• Similarly, with "did", the main verb always reverts to the base form: "He did not went" (incorrect) vs "He did not go" (correct).

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Teachers 1_________ given continuous opportunities for self-improvement and to learn the latest innovations and advances in their professions. Each teacher 2_________ expected to participate in at least 50 hours of CPD opportunities every year for their own professional development, driven 3_________ their own interests. CPD opportunities will, in particular, 4_________ cover the latest pedagogies regarding foundational literacy and numeracy, formative and adaptive assessment of learning outcomes, competency-based learning and related pedagogies, 5_________ experiential learning, arts-integrated, sports-integrated and storytelling-based approaches, etc.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. will be.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb form to complete the passive structure **"Teachers _____ given continuous opportunities..."**, describing a general, ongoing policy/commitment about the future.

• Rule — Simple Future Passive: Subject + will be + V3 (past participle) is used to express a general future action, plan, or policy statement, matching the formal, prospective tone of the passage (a document describing what CPD opportunities "will" involve).

• "will be given" correctly completes the passive verb phrase and fits the overall future-tense tone used consistently across the passage (compare "CPD opportunities will, in particular, cover...").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "shall be" is grammatically usable in formal/legal English (mainly with "I/we") but is stylistically inconsistent with the passage's established use of "will" throughout; it does not match the passage's tone.

• Option 3: "can be" is incorrect because it expresses ability/possibility, not a definite future policy commitment, changing the intended meaning.

• Option 4: "would be" is incorrect because "would" is typically used for a hypothetical, conditional, or past-future sense, not for a straightforward future statement of policy.

NOTE

• In formal policy/administrative writing, "will" is the standard modal for stating future plans, entitlements, and provisions.

• Consistency of tense/modal usage across a passage is a key clue in cloze-passage questions — look for parallel structures elsewhere in the passage (here, "CPD opportunities will...cover" confirms the future tense pattern).

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Teachers 1_________ given continuous opportunities for self-improvement and to learn the latest innovations and advances in their professions. Each teacher 2_________ expected to participate in at least 50 hours of CPD opportunities every year for their own professional development, driven 3_________ their own interests. CPD opportunities will, in particular, 4_________ cover the latest pedagogies regarding foundational literacy and numeracy, formative and adaptive assessment of learning outcomes, competency-based learning and related pedagogies, 5_________ experiential learning, arts-integrated, sports-integrated and storytelling-based approaches, etc.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. will be.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the passive structure **"Each teacher _____ expected to participate..."**, again describing a general future requirement/policy.

• Rule — Simple Future Passive: Subject + will be + V3 is used for a general future obligation or expectation, consistent with the passage's overall future-tense, policy-document style (as also seen in blank 1, "Teachers will be given...").

• "will be expected" correctly and consistently completes the sentence, matching the tense pattern of the rest of the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "shall be" does not match the passage's consistent use of "will" and is stylistically inconsistent with the rest of the passage.

• Option 2: "would be" is incorrect because "would" suggests a hypothetical or conditional expectation, not a straightforward future one.

• Option 3: "can be" is incorrect because it expresses mere possibility/ability rather than a definite future expectation, which changes the meaning intended by the passage.

NOTE

• Cloze passages frequently repeat the same grammatical pattern across multiple blanks (here, both blank 1 and blank 2 use the future passive "will be + V3") — spotting this parallelism helps confirm the correct option.

• Distinguish carefully between "will" (simple future/general statement), "would" (hypothetical/past future), "can" (ability/possibility) and "shall" (formal future, mainly I/we) when solving such blanks.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Teachers 1_________ given continuous opportunities for self-improvement and to learn the latest innovations and advances in their professions. Each teacher 2_________ expected to participate in at least 50 hours of CPD opportunities every year for their own professional development, driven 3_________ their own interests. CPD opportunities will, in particular, 4_________ cover the latest pedagogies regarding foundational literacy and numeracy, formative and adaptive assessment of learning outcomes, competency-based learning and related pedagogies, 5_________ experiential learning, arts-integrated, sports-integrated and storytelling-based approaches, etc.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. by.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in the phrase **"driven _____ their own interests"**, which requires the correct preposition to complete the passive expression "driven by".

• Rule — Fixed preposition with "driven" (passive sense): The verb "drive", when used passively to mean "motivated/propelled by something", is always followed by the preposition "by" — e.g. "driven by passion", "driven by ambition", "driven by their own interests".

• No other preposition fits idiomatically with "driven" in this sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "from" is incorrect; "driven from" would imply being forced out of/expelled from a place, which does not fit the intended meaning here.

• Option 3: "at" is incorrect; "at" does not combine idiomatically with "driven" to express motivation or cause.

• Option 4: "for" is incorrect; "for" does not combine idiomatically with "driven" in this passive sense.

NOTE

• Other common "verb + by" collocations tested by SSC: motivated by, inspired by, influenced by, guided by, prompted by.

• Confusing "driven by" (cause/motivation) with "driven from" (expulsion) or "driven to" (a resulting state, e.g. "driven to despair") is a common trap — always check the intended meaning of the sentence.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Teachers 1_________ given continuous opportunities for self-improvement and to learn the latest innovations and advances in their professions. Each teacher 2_________ expected to participate in at least 50 hours of CPD opportunities every year for their own professional development, driven 3_________ their own interests. CPD opportunities will, in particular, 4_________ cover the latest pedagogies regarding foundational literacy and numeracy, formative and adaptive assessment of learning outcomes, competency-based learning and related pedagogies, 5_________ experiential learning, arts-integrated, sports-integrated and storytelling-based approaches, etc.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. systematically.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"CPD opportunities will, in particular, _____ cover the latest pedagogies..."**, describing how a wide, structured range of topics (foundational literacy and numeracy, assessment, competency-based learning, etc.) will be addressed.

• Rule — Context-based adverb selection: The adverb must logically match the formal, organised, policy-document tone of the passage, and describe a planned, methodical, well-organised process rather than a haphazard one.

• "systematically" (in an organised, methodical, step-by-step manner) is the only option consistent with the formal and comprehensive coverage of pedagogical topics described in the rest of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "carelessly" is incorrect because it means "without care or attention", which directly contradicts the serious, formal tone of a policy document about teacher training.

• Option 3: "roughly" is incorrect because it suggests an approximate or imprecise coverage, which does not fit the detailed and structured list of topics that follows.

• Option 4: "partially" is incorrect because it means "incompletely", whereas the sentence lists a comprehensive range of topics meant to be fully covered.

NOTE

• In formal/administrative passages, look for adverbs that match the register and intent of the text — words implying carelessness or incompleteness are usually distractors.

• Common formal adverbs tested by SSC: systematically, comprehensively, effectively, adequately, rigorously.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Teachers 1_________ given continuous opportunities for self-improvement and to learn the latest innovations and advances in their professions. Each teacher 2_________ expected to participate in at least 50 hours of CPD opportunities every year for their own professional development, driven 3_________ their own interests. CPD opportunities will, in particular, 4_________ cover the latest pedagogies regarding foundational literacy and numeracy, formative and adaptive assessment of learning outcomes, competency-based learning and related pedagogies, 5_________ experiential learning, arts-integrated, sports-integrated and storytelling-based approaches, etc.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. such as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"...competency-based learning and related pedagogies, _____ experiential learning, arts-integrated, sports-integrated and storytelling-based approaches, etc."**, where a list of specific examples is being introduced.

• Rule — "such as" to introduce examples: The phrase "such as" is used to introduce specific examples of a general category that has just been mentioned ("related pedagogies, such as experiential learning, arts-integrated...approaches").

• The presence of a list of concrete examples (experiential learning, arts-integrated, sports-integrated, storytelling-based approaches) followed by "etc." strongly signals that an example-introducing phrase like "such as" is required.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "same as" is incorrect because it implies identity/equivalence between two things, not an example relationship.

• Option 3: "from as" is incorrect; this is not a standard English phrase and is grammatically invalid here.

• Option 4: "for as" is incorrect; this is not a standard English phrase and is grammatically invalid here.

NOTE

• Common example-introducing phrases in English: "such as", "for example", "for instance", "like", "namely".

• Do not confuse "such as" (introducing examples of a category) with "as such" (meaning "in itself" or "therefore"), which have very different meanings and uses.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The waters of Germany are abundant in fish, but there are few genera and species in them.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. deficient.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "abundant" means existing or available in large quantities; plentiful (प्रचुर मात्रा में उपलब्ध).

• The antonym "deficient" means lacking in some quality or element that is necessary or usual; insufficient (अपर्याप्त/कमी वाला), which is the direct opposite of "abundant".
◦ Example: The soil in this region is deficient in nitrogen, unlike the abundant fertile land nearby.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "flourish" (फलना-फूलना): To grow or develop successfully; this is unrelated in meaning and is a verb, not a matching antonym for the adjective "abundant".

• Option 3: "allay" (शांत करना): To diminish or put at rest a fear, doubt, or worry; unrelated to the idea of quantity.

• Option 4: "discord" (मतभेद): Disagreement or conflict between people; unrelated to the idea of quantity or scarcity.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "abundant": plentiful, ample, copious, bountiful, profuse.

• Other antonyms of "abundant" commonly tested: scarce, scanty, sparse, meagre, insufficient.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Revolution
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Gyration.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Revolution", apart from its common political sense, also means a single complete circular turn or rotation around an axis or a central point (एक चक्कर/परिक्रमा), as in "the earth's revolution around the sun".

• "Gyration" means a circular or spiral motion; the act of rotating or whirling (घूर्णन), which matches this sense of "revolution" as a rotating movement.
◦ Example: The dancer's rapid gyrations around the stage mesmerised the audience, much like a planet's revolution around its star.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Stagnation" (ठहराव): A state of not moving, developing, or progressing; this is nearly opposite to the idea of a turning/rotating motion.

• Option 3: "Harmony" (सामंजस्य): Agreement or a pleasing combination of elements; unrelated to rotational movement.

• Option 4: "Order" (व्यवस्था): A state of arrangement or sequence; unrelated to rotational movement.

NOTE

• SSC often tests the lesser-used, non-political meanings of common words — here "revolution" is tested in its scientific/physical sense of "a turn or rotation", not its political sense of "a forcible overthrow".

• Related words: rotation, revolve, orbit, spin, whirl.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM for the given word.
Ghastly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Pleasant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Ghastly" means causing great horror or fear; extremely unpleasant or shocking to look at (भयानक/डरावना).

• The antonym "Pleasant" means giving a sense of happy satisfaction or enjoyment; agreeable and likeable (सुखद/मनभावन), which is the direct opposite of something horrifying or gruesome.
◦ Example: After the ghastly accident scene, the pleasant view of the countryside came as a great relief.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Agitated" (उत्तेजित): Feeling or appearing troubled or nervous; this is not an opposite of "ghastly" — in fact, something ghastly could well leave a person agitated.

• Option 2: "Bitter" (कडवा): Having a sharp, unpleasant taste, or feeling resentment; this carries a negative connotation similar to "ghastly", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Relaxing" (आरामदायक): Causing one to feel calm and free from tension; this is close in meaning to "pleasant" but describes an effect rather than a quality, making "Pleasant" the more precise, direct antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "ghastly": horrifying, gruesome, dreadful, hideous, macabre.

• Other antonyms of "ghastly" commonly tested: delightful, charming, appealing, lovely.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.
I opened the box beneath the table and took of a book, the Materia Medica.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. took out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "took of" is grammatically incorrect and meaningless; there is no phrasal verb "take of" in English.

• Rule — Correct phrasal verb for "to remove/retrieve something from somewhere": The correct phrasal verb is "take out" (past tense: "took out"), meaning to remove or extract something from a place.

• Since the sentence describes the subject retrieving a book from inside the box, "took out" is the only option that both exists as a standard English phrasal verb and fits the meaning of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "take off" is incorrect; besides being in the wrong tense (the sentence needs the past tense to match "opened"), "take off" means to remove clothing/an aircraft to leave the ground, not to retrieve an object from a container.

• Option 3: "took in" is incorrect; "take in" means to absorb, understand, or deceive someone, which does not fit the context of retrieving a book from a box.

• Option 4: "No substitution required" is incorrect because "took of" is not a valid English expression and must be corrected.

NOTE

• Common "take" phrasal verbs tested by SSC: take out (remove), take off (remove clothing/depart), take in (absorb/deceive), take up (start a hobby/occupy), take after (resemble), take over (assume control).

• Always check that the tense of the substituted phrasal verb matches the rest of the sentence (here, the past tense "opened" requires "took out", not the base form "take out").

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a spelling error.
I was alarmed lest we should be wreked.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. be wreked.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "wreked" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "wrecked" — meaning destroyed or badly damaged, especially as a result of an accident.
◦ Example: The storm wrecked several boats along the coast.

• Spelling key: WRECK + ED. The base word "wreck" already contains the double consonant cluster "ck", which must be retained before adding the "-ed" suffix; "wreked" incorrectly drops the "c".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "I was" is correctly spelt.

• Option 3: "we should" is correctly spelt.

• Option 4: "alarmed lest" is correctly spelt.

NOTE

• "Lest" is a conjunction meaning "in case; for fear that", commonly followed by "should" (e.g. "He ran fast lest he should miss the train").

• Other commonly misspelt "-ck" words tested by SSC: check, track, attack, struck, knocked — the "ck" cluster is frequently and incorrectly reduced to a single "k" by candidates.

question:
Based on the situation in the sentence, select the most appropriate idiom.
After many years of rivalry, the two schools decided to ________ and participate in a National Event together.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. bury the hatchet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "bury the hatchet" means to stop fighting or arguing with someone and become friendly again; to make peace after a quarrel or rivalry (मतभेद भुलाकर मेल-मिलाप करना).
◦ Example: The two neighbours finally decided to bury the hatchet and attend each other's family functions.

• The idiom originates from a Native American custom of literally burying a tomahawk (hatchet) as a symbol of ending hostilities and making peace.

• The situation in the sentence — two rival schools coming together after years of rivalry to participate in an event jointly — exactly matches the sense of ending a conflict and reconciling.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "bell the cat" (जोखिम भरा कार्य स्वयं करना): To undertake a difficult or dangerous task on behalf of a group; unrelated to reconciliation.

• Option 3: "go cold turkey" (अचानक आदत छोड़ना): To suddenly and completely stop doing something, especially giving up an addictive habit; unrelated to the context of rivalry.

• Option 4: "be in the doldrums" (निराशा/उदासी की स्थिति में होना): To be in a state of inactivity, stagnation, or low spirits; unrelated to the idea of making peace.

NOTE

• Other idioms of reconciliation/peace-making tested by SSC: "to make amends", "to patch up", "to let bygones be bygones", "to turn over a new leaf".

question:
Choose the option that best describes the meaning of the idioms and phrases underlined in the given sentence.
A jack of all trades cannot survive in the world of specialisation.
option_2: A person who can do many things but is not an expert in any
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A person who can do many things but is not an expert in any.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a jack of all trades" refers to a person who can do many different kinds of work reasonably well but is not a specialist or expert in any single one of them (कई कामों में हाथ आजमाने वाला पर किसी में भी विशेषज्ञ न होने वाला व्यक्ति).
◦ Example: As the office's jack of all trades, he handles accounts, repairs computers, and manages events, but is not formally trained in any of these.

• The full traditional saying is "Jack of all trades, master of none", which emphasises that such versatility usually comes at the cost of true mastery in any one field — this matches the sentence's context, where such a person "cannot survive in the world of specialisation".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A good communicator" is incorrect; the idiom is about versatility in skills or trades, not communication ability.

• Option 3: "An expert of many jobs" is incorrect and in fact contradicts the idiom's meaning — a "jack of all trades" is explicitly NOT an expert, but a generalist.

• Option 4: "A businessman" is incorrect; the idiom does not refer to any specific profession such as business.

NOTE

• Other idioms about versatility/skill tested by SSC: "a Jack of all trades, master of none" (full version), "an all-rounder", "a man for all seasons" (a versatile, adaptable person).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Do not later about the street.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. loiter around.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "later about" is meaningless in this context; the intended word is "loiter", meaning to stand or wait around in a public place without an obvious purpose (बिना किसी काम के इधर-उधर घूमना/मंडराना).
◦ Example: The security guard asked the boys not to loiter around the entrance.

• "Loiter around" correctly conveys the intended meaning of aimlessly hanging about the street, matching the warning tone of the sentence "Do not...the street".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "litre about" is incorrect; "litre" is a unit of volume and has no connection to the intended meaning.

• Option 3: "litter about" is incorrect; "litter" means to scatter rubbish untidily, which does not fit the context of the sentence.

• Option 4: "latter about" is incorrect; "latter" means "the second of two things mentioned" and does not fit grammatically or semantically here.

NOTE

• Commonly confused words with "loiter": litter (scatter rubbish), litre (unit of volume), latter (the second of two), later (at a future time) — these are frequently used as distractors in SSC vocabulary questions due to their similar spelling/sound.

• Synonyms of "loiter": linger, dawdle, saunter, hang about.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Compulsory
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Optional.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Compulsory" means required by law or a rule; obligatory; something that must be done (अनिवार्य).

• The antonym "Optional" means available to be chosen but not obligatory; not compulsory (वैकल्पिक), which is the direct opposite of "compulsory".
◦ Example: Attendance at the morning assembly is compulsory, but joining the extra sports session is optional.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Reliable" (भरोसेमंद): Able to be trusted; unrelated to the idea of obligation or choice.

• Option 3: "Factional" (गुटबाजी से संबंधित): Relating to a small organised group within a larger one; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "Full-fledged" (पूर्ण रूप से विकसित): Fully developed or complete; unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "compulsory": mandatory, obligatory, required, essential.

• Other antonyms of "compulsory" commonly tested: voluntary, elective, discretionary.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Well, I prefer eating at home from eating out.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. to eating out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "from eating out" is grammatically incorrect; the verb "prefer", when comparing two alternatives using gerunds (verb + -ing forms), must be followed by the preposition "to", not "from".

• Rule — "prefer X to Y": When comparing two things or activities with the verb "prefer", the correct structure is "prefer + gerund/noun + to + gerund/noun", e.g. "I prefer tea to coffee", "She prefers reading to watching TV".

• Applying the rule: "I prefer eating at home to eating out" is the grammatically correct comparative structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "and eating out" is incorrect; "and" merely joins the two activities rather than expressing a comparative preference, which changes the intended meaning of the sentence.

• Option 2: "than eating out" is incorrect; "than" is used for comparisons with comparative adjectives/adverbs (e.g. "better than"), not directly after "prefer".

• Option 3: "while eating out" is incorrect; "while" indicates simultaneous action, not comparison/preference, and does not fit the intended meaning.

NOTE

• Common confusion: "would rather X than Y" takes "than", while "prefer X to Y" takes "to" — candidates often wrongly mix these two structures.

• Other fixed-preposition verb patterns tested by SSC: "differ from", "compare to/with", "superior to", "senior to".

question:
Rectify the sentence by selecting the correct spelling from the options.
The advertisement of vacencies in education sector has received huge response.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Vacancies.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Vacancies" — the plural of "vacancy", meaning unoccupied positions or posts available for employment. (रिक्तियां)
◦ Example: The company announced several vacancies for the post of data analyst.

• Spelling key: VA + CAN + CIES. Note the vowel "a" (not "e") in the first syllable, the consonant sequence "c-a-n" in the middle, and the ending "-cies" (not "-sies") when forming the plural of a noun ending in "-cy".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Vecencies" is incorrect; the first two vowels have been wrongly changed from "a" to "e".

• Option 2: "Vacansies" is incorrect; the middle consonant has been wrongly changed from "c" to "s".

• Option 3: "Vecancies" is incorrect; the first vowel has been wrongly changed from "a" to "e".

NOTE

• Nouns ending in "-cy" form their plural by changing "y" to "ies": vacancy → vacancies, policy → policies, agency → agencies.

• Other commonly misspelt words with the "a" vs "e" confusion tested by SSC: separate, definite, category, necessary.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The athlete looked unsettled before the race.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Confident.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "unsettled" means anxious, uneasy, or lacking composure; not calm (बेचैन/अस्थिर मनःस्थिति).

• The antonym "Confident" means feeling or showing certainty about oneself or one's abilities; self-assured (आत्मविश्वासी), which is the direct opposite of feeling anxious or uneasy.
◦ Example: Despite looking unsettled during warm-up, the athlete appeared confident once the race began.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Reticent" (मितभाषी/चुप रहने वाला): Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reserved in speech — this is a different quality altogether, not an opposite of "unsettled".

• Option 3: "Triumphant" (विजयी): Feeling or showing great happiness after a victory; describes a post-success emotion, not composure beforehand.

• Option 4: "Tangent" (स्पर्शरेखा/असंबद्ध विषय): A completely unrelated topic or, in geometry, a line touching a curve at one point; unrelated in meaning to "unsettled".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "unsettled": anxious, restless, uneasy, agitated, nervous.

• Other antonyms of "unsettled" commonly tested: composed, calm, steady, assured, poised.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Candid
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Honest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Candid" means truthful and straightforward; frank, especially about something that might be uncomfortable to hear (स्पष्टवादी/निष्कपट).

• "Honest" means free of deceit and untruthfulness; sincere and truthful (ईमानदार), which closely matches the meaning of "candid".
◦ Example: She gave a candid, honest opinion about the flaws in the proposal, even though it was unwelcome.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Cruel" (क्रूर): Deliberately causing pain or suffering; unrelated to the idea of frankness or honesty.

• Option 2: "Bright" (चमकीला/तेज़ बुद्धि वाला): Emitting light, or intelligent; unrelated in meaning to "candid".

• Option 3: "Top" (शीर्ष): The highest point or rank; unrelated in meaning to "candid".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "candid": frank, forthright, sincere, outspoken, straightforward.

• Antonyms of "candid" commonly tested: evasive, dishonest, secretive, deceitful.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The artist received a ____________ from the audience.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. round of applause.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires the correct collocation used with the noun "applause" to describe the audience's response to the artist's performance.

• Rule — Fixed collocation: The standard, idiomatic phrase in English is "a round of applause", meaning a burst of clapping by a group of people to show appreciation.

• No other quantifying word listed conventionally collocates with "applause" in standard English.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "handful of applause" is incorrect; "handful of" is conventionally used with countable items (e.g. "a handful of people"), not with an abstract mass noun like "applause".

• Option 3: "bunch of applause" is incorrect; "bunch of" is conventionally used with groups of countable objects (e.g. "a bunch of flowers"), not with "applause".

• Option 4: "plenty of applause" is incorrect; although grammatically permissible in a general sense, it is not the fixed, idiomatic collocation used to describe a burst of clapping and does not fit as naturally as "a round of applause".

NOTE

• Other fixed "a/an ___ of ___" collocations tested by SSC: a bout of illness, a fit of anger, a peal of laughter, a flash of lightning, a spell of rain.

• "A round of applause" specifically implies a single, collective burst of clapping — commonly used after a speech or performance.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
The experienced surgeon handled the delicate procedure with care and precision.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. seasoned.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "experienced" means having gained knowledge or skill from doing something over a period of time; skilled as a result of practice (अनुभवी).

• "Seasoned" means experienced in a particular activity through long practice; accustomed and skilled (अनुभवी/परिपक्व), which is a close and appropriate substitute for "experienced" in this context.
◦ Example: As a seasoned surgeon with over twenty years of practice, she handled the complex operation calmly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "amateur" (शौकिया/अनुभवहीन): A person who engages in an activity without professional skill or as a hobbyist; this means the opposite of "experienced" and contradicts the sentence's description of care and precision.

• Option 3: "untrained" (अप्रशिक्षित): Not having received training; this is the opposite of "experienced" and would contradict the careful, precise handling described.

• Option 4: "unskilled" (अकुशल): Lacking skill or expertise; this too is the opposite of "experienced" and would contradict the sentence's meaning.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "experienced": skilled, expert, practised, veteran, accomplished.

• Antonyms of "experienced" commonly tested: inexperienced, novice, amateur, untrained, green.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
I have left it to his discretion to accept or decline my offer.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Inattention.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "discretion" means the freedom and careful, prudent judgment to decide or act on one's own in a given situation (विवेकपूर्ण निर्णय लेने की स्वतंत्रता/समझदारी).

• The antonym "Inattention" means lack of care, attention, or thoughtfulness; carelessness (असावधानी/लापरवाही), which is the opposite of the careful, considered judgment implied by "discretion".
◦ Example: His discretion in handling the delicate matter was praised, unlike his colleague's inattention to similar issues in the past.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Wisdom" (बुद्धिमत्ता): Deep understanding and good sense; this is close in meaning to "discretion" (careful judgment), making it a near-synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 2: "Calculation" (सोच-विचार): Careful and thoughtful planning; this too is close in sense to careful judgment, not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Judgement" (निर्णय-क्षमता): The ability to make considered decisions; "discretion" is essentially a form of sound judgement, so this option is a near-synonym, not an antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "discretion": prudence, tact, judgement, circumspection, wisdom.

• Other antonyms of "discretion" commonly tested: indiscretion, carelessness, recklessness, imprudence.
